title: What Transfers Across Cuneiform? Script-Level Substrate and Language-Specific Regularities via Segmentation and Representation
abstract: arXiv:2611.19094v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Cuneiform recorded typologically unrelated languages for more than three millennia, raising a natural question: which of its statistical regularities are properties of the shared writing system, and which belong to individual languages? We answer this with two probe pairs targeting the same script-versus-language decomposition. The first compares two unsupervised, dictionary-free segmentation methods: transitional probability (TP), grounded in infant statistical-learning research, and Morfessor. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic evaluation of dictionary-free segmentation on cuneiform; the only prior published baseline relies on a hand-built dictionary (Max-Match, F1 = 0.74). Both our methods reach F1 > 0.97 within language (Morfessor reaches F1 > 0.99 on Akkadian and Sumerian), exceeding MaxMatch by more than 23 F1 points, but diverge sharply in cross-language transfer: TP holds F1 > 0.95 across all six language pairs, while

translated_title: 什么在楔形文字间可迁移？通过分割与表征探究文字层面的底层共性及语言特有规律
translated_abstract: 楔形文字记录了类型学上互不相关的语言长达三千余年，这引发了一个自然的问题：其统计规律中哪些属于共享书写系统的性质，哪些属于个别语言的性质？我们通过针对同一文字-语言分解问题的两组探针实验来回答这一问题。第一组比较了两种无监督、无需词典的分割方法：基于婴儿统计学习研究的迁移概率法（TP）和 Morfessor。据我们所知，这是首次在楔形文字上对无词典分割进行系统评估；此前唯一已发表的基线依赖于人工构建的词典（Max-Match，F1 = 0.74）。我们的两种方法在语言内均达到 F1 > 0.97（Morfessor 在阿卡德语和苏美尔语上达到 F1 > 0.99），比 MaxMatch 高出 23 个以上 F1 点，但在跨语言迁移方面二者差异显著：TP 在全部六个语言对上均保持 F1 > 0.95，而（原文摘要在此处截断，后续内容缺失）
tldr: 本文首次对楔形文字开展了无词典无监督分割的系统评估，发现 TP 和 Morfessor 在语言内均大幅超越基于词典的基线，但只有基于迁移概率的方法能够跨语言稳定迁移，从而区分了楔形文字中共享书写系统层面的底层规律与各语言特有的规律。
en_tdlr: This paper presents the first systematic evaluation of dictionary-free unsupervised segmentation on cuneiform, showing that TP and Morfessor both far exceed the dictionary-based baseline within languages, while only the transitional-probability approach transfers robustly across languages, thereby distinguishing script-level substrate regularities from language-specific ones.
